```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

The two assembly strategies in `2023-05-12` yielded very different assemblies,
due to the last, polishing step. Many contigs were filtered out when the
polishing was performed with Nanopore reads. The `flye` logs in
`../2023-05-12/flye/*/flye.log` indicate a number of differences between
the polishing steps of the two assemblies:

 |                                   |  PB_ONT    |   ONT_PB   |
 | ----------------------------------|------------|------------|
 | Number of bubbles generated       |  3242914   |  11086641  |
 | Long bubbles splitted             |   301193   |     12526  |
 | Empty bubbles skipped             |   357710   |      7562  |
 | Long-branch bubbles skipped       |      418   |       461  |
 | Alignment error                   | 0.127446   |  0.160949  |
 | Mean contig coverage              |        2   |         7  |
 | Filtered contigs                  |    14069   |      1176  |
 | Total length of filtered contigs  | 70456427   |   4026484  |
 | Unpolished sequences remining     |    20929   |      1962  |

```{r}
library('Biostrings')
library('MetBrewer')
nanopo <- read.table('../2023-05-12/flye/ONT_PB/assembly_info.txt',
                     col.names = c('ctg', 'len', 'cov', 'circ', 'rep',
                                   'mult', 'group', 'path'))
pacbio <- read.table('../2023-05-12/flye/PB_ONT/assembly_info.txt',
                     col.names = c('ctg', 'len', 'cov', 'circ', 'rep',
                                   'mult', 'group', 'path'))
nanopoMult <- table(nanopo[, c('mult', 'cov')])
barplot(nanopoMult[1:5, 1:23], col = met.brewer('Egypt', 5),
        main = 'Nanopore', xlab = 'Coverage', ylab = 'Num. of contigs')
legend(23, 4500, c('1', '2', '3', '4', '5'),
       fill = met.brewer('Egypt', 5), title = 'Multiplicity')

pacbioMult <- table(pacbio[, c('mult', 'cov')])
barplot(pacbioMult[1:5, 1:23], col = met.brewer('Egypt', 5),
        main = 'PacBio', xlab = 'Coverage', ylab = 'Num. of contigs')
legend(23, 600, c('1', '2', '3', '4', '5'),
       fill = met.brewer('Egypt', 5), title = 'Multiplicity')

nanopoAss <- readDNAStringSet('../2023-05-12/flye/ONT_PB/assembly.fasta')
pacbioAss <- readDNAStringSet('../2023-05-12/flye/PB_ONT/assembly.fasta')
if (! file.exists('nano_n1lin.fasta')) {
   writeXStringSet(nanopoAss[nanopo[nanopo$mult == 1 & nanopo$circ == 'N', 'ctg']],
                   'nano_n1lin.fasta')
}
if (! file.exists('nano_n1cir.fasta')) {
   writeXStringSet(nanopoAss[nanopo[nanopo$mult == 1 & nanopo$circ == 'Y', 'ctg']],
                   'nano_n1cir.fasta')
}
if (! file.exists('pacbio_n1lin.fasta')) {
   writeXStringSet(pacbioAss[pacbio[pacbio$mult == 1 & pacbio$circ == 'N', 'ctg']],
                   'pacbio_n1lin.fasta')
}
if (! file.exists('pacbio_n1cir.fasta')) {
   writeXStringSet(pacbioAss[pacbio[pacbio$mult == 1 & pacbio$circ == 'Y', 'ctg']],
                   'pacbio_n1cir.fasta')
}
```

The plots above suggest most of the contigs with coverage below
10 are unique, not repeated, sequences. But the highly
covered contigs, most with a coverage of exactly 20 (!) may
be a mixture of different multiplicities, according to `flye`.
I ignore the reasons a contig gets a multiplicity assigned,
but they seem to be different from the reason to classify a
contig as *repeatitive*. I suggest we use only contigs
of multiplicity 1, both circular and linear. Among the *circular*
ones, I expect the mitochondrial genome to be.

I do not find evidences of the split of allelic sequences due
to high heterozygosity, yet.
